title: Insertion Anomaly
description: Recognize insertion anomalies in course enrollment data, separate independent facts, preserve foreign-key integrity, and query courses with zero registrations.

questions.question_text: StudentCourse has primary key(StudentID, CourseID) and instructor detail columns. Why cannot it record a new instructor with no enrollment when those key values are unknown?
options: Because InstructorName does not allow duplicate values
Because StudentID and CourseID are part of the table's key and cannot be left null, but no enrollment exists yet to supply them
Because the table has a maximum row limit
Because InstructorOffice must always match an existing CourseName
questions.explanation: Since (StudentID, CourseID) forms the primary key, entity integrity forbids null key values — so a row with no student and no course cannot be inserted, even though it's the instructor's data that needs recording.

questions.question_text: What is the insertion anomaly, precisely?
options: The inability to insert two rows with the same primary key
The inability to insert a fact about one entity without also having unrelated data required by the key of another entity
A performance slowdown when inserting many rows at once
An error thrown when inserting NULL into a non-key column
questions.explanation: It specifically describes being blocked from recording a valid fact (like a new instructor) because the schema forces an unrelated fact (an enrollment) to exist first.

questions.question_text: A new course 'Cloud Computing' (C5) has been approved and assigned instructor I2, but no student has enrolled yet. What happens in the unnormalized schema?
options: The course can be inserted normally with StudentID left blank
The course's existence cannot be recorded until at least one student enrolls, because StudentID is part of the required key
The course is automatically assigned a placeholder student
This scenario cannot occur because CourseID is not part of the key
questions.explanation: Just like the instructor case, a course's own facts (CourseName, its instructor) are trapped behind the need for an enrollment row, so it can't be inserted independently.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a commonly attempted but flawed workaround for the insertion anomaly?
options: Adding a foreign key constraint
Inserting placeholder/fake values like StudentID='PENDING' to satisfy the key requirement
Normalizing the table into Student, Course, and Instructor relations
Adding an index on InstructorID
questions.explanation: Using fake placeholder key values avoids the immediate error but corrupts the key's meaning and pollutes future queries — it's a workaround, not a real fix; the real fix is decomposition (2NF/3NF).

questions.question_text: Which schema change genuinely eliminates the insertion anomaly for instructor data?
options: Making InstructorOffice nullable
Creating a separate Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice) relation so instructor facts can be inserted independent of any enrollment
Adding a unique constraint on InstructorName
Removing the EnrollmentDate column
questions.explanation: Once Instructor is its own relation keyed by InstructorID, a new instructor row can be inserted with no dependency on StudentID/CourseID at all — this is exactly the 3NF decomposition covered later.

questions.question_text: Is 'rejecting a duplicate primary key insert' the same thing as an insertion anomaly?
options: Yes, they are identical concepts
No — a duplicate-key rejection is a normal integrity constraint working correctly; the insertion anomaly is about being unable to record a valid, non-duplicate fact at all
Yes, because both involve the INSERT statement
No — insertion anomalies only happen with UPDATE statements
questions.explanation: A duplicate-key rejection is the database correctly enforcing uniqueness. The insertion anomaly is a design flaw that blocks a legitimate, unique fact from being stored because of an unrelated missing key component.

questions.question_text: In that StudentCourse design with primary key(StudentID, CourseID), why does allowing NULL InstructorOffice not make an instructor-only row with missing student/course keys valid?
options: Because InstructorOffice was never nullable in any schema
Because the blocking columns (StudentID, CourseID) are part of the primary key, and entity integrity forbids null primary key components regardless of other columns' nullability
Because NULL values are illegal in all relational databases
Because it would violate 3NF
questions.explanation: The problem isn't that InstructorOffice can't be null — it's that the *key* columns (StudentID, CourseID) can't be null, and those are exactly the values missing when only instructor data is known.

questions.question_text: In terms of root cause, the insertion anomaly is best described as:
options: An unrelated, independent flaw from data redundancy
A direct symptom of storing multiple entities' facts (student, course, instructor) in one table keyed by an unrelated composite key
A hardware limitation of the database engine
A consequence of using auto-incrementing keys
questions.explanation: Because instructor and course facts are riding along in a table keyed by (StudentID, CourseID), any entity's data that isn't yet tied to an enrollment cannot be inserted — the same redundancy from 21.1 causes this.

questions.question_text: Which situation is an insertion anomaly?
options: A course cannot be stored until a student enrollment is invented
A duplicate enrollment is correctly rejected
A missing foreign key parent is correctly rejected
A SELECT returns sorted courses
questions.explanation: The schema prevents a valid independent fact from being represented.

questions.question_text: Why is a fake student row a poor fix for a new course?
options: It guarantees normalization
It asserts participation that did not occur
It removes all duplicate titles
It creates a real enrollment automatically
questions.explanation: Invented participation corrupts the meaning of stored facts.

questions.question_text: Which relation should own course_title in the stated model?
options: enrollments
courses
A fake student table
Only a report cache
questions.explanation: Course attributes belong with course identity.

questions.question_text: What does course_id determine under the simplified rule?
options: Every enrolled student identifier
All unrelated course identifiers
course_title and instructor
The current SELECT order
questions.explanation: The rule assigns one title and instructor per course.

questions.question_text: Why retain a unique student_id, course_id pair?
options: To prevent empty courses
To force every course to have a student
To make names globally unique
To prevent duplicate enrollment for the stated business rule
questions.explanation: The relationship has its own business uniqueness.

questions.question_text: Which query naturally finds courses with no enrollments?
options: A courses query with correlated NOT EXISTS
An inner join requiring enrollment
A filter student_id = NULL
A query of students alone
questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS tests the absence of matching participation.

questions.question_text: Why use COUNT(e.student_id) in a course left join?
options: It counts a missing match as one
It counts actual enrollment matches
It makes every course count equal
It removes courses without students
questions.explanation: A nonnullable child field is NULL only for the unmatched outer row.

questions.question_text: Are repeated course titles always invalid?
options: Yes, titles are always global keys
Only when there are no students
No, different courses may share a title
Only when a view is used
questions.explanation: Identity rules come from the business rather than labels alone.

questions.question_text: What must happen before collapsing conflicting titles for one course ID?
options: Select an arbitrary title silently
Delete the course automatically
Invent another student
Investigate and approve the correct course fact
questions.explanation: Conflicting dependency values need an explicit resolution.

questions.question_text: Can course existence be required without requiring an enrollment?
options: Yes, store a course row independently
No, all entities need a child row
Only with fake identifiers
Only if keys are removed
questions.explanation: Separate entity and relationship relations allow independent lifecycles.

questions.question_text: If courses have term specific instructors, what should be reconsidered?
options: Only the font size
The dependency and offering model
Only the order of columns
Whether SELECT supports aliases
questions.explanation: The simplified course-to-instructor dependency may not hold.

questions.question_text: Does adding a surrogate enrollment ID alone remove the anomaly?
options: Yes, every surrogate normalizes all facts
Yes, NULL becomes a course
No, independent facts still need proper owners
Only when IDs are text
questions.explanation: A new row identifier does not separate mixed fact types.

coding_problems.title: Find Courses Without Enrollment
coding_problems.task: Return course_id and course_title for courses with no enrollment. Order by course_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY,course_title VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL,PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,'Databases'),(20,'Networks'),(30,'Security'); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10),(2,10),(1,20);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT c.course_id,c.course_title FROM courses c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.course_id=c.course_id) ORDER BY c.course_id;
coding_problems.ordering: Order rows by the key specified in the task.
edge_cases: Empty input returns no detail rows.
Include equal values on different source rows.
Verify boundary and NULL handling when the schema permits them.
hints: Determine the result grain before writing the query.
Use explicit projected columns and a final ORDER BY.
coding_problems.explanation: The solution implements the stated row selection and preserves the requested result grain; the final ordering makes comparisons deterministic.

coding_problems.title: Count Every Course Enrollment
coding_problems.task: Return course_id, course_title, enrollment_count for every course, including zero. Order by course_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY,course_title VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL,PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,'Databases'),(20,'Networks'),(30,'Security'); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10),(2,10),(1,20);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT c.course_id,c.course_title,COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrollment_count FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id=c.course_id GROUP BY c.course_id,c.course_title ORDER BY c.course_id;
coding_problems.expected:
course_id	course_title	enrollment_count
10	Databases	2
20	Networks	1
30	Security	0

notes:
## When one fact cannot exist without another

A college wants to announce a new course before any student enrolls. Its only table contains student_id, course_id, course_title, and instructor. The primary key is the pair student_id and course_id. A real course exists, but the design has nowhere to record it without also inventing a student enrollment. This is an insertion anomaly: the structure prevents an independent valid fact from being stored unless an unrelated fact is supplied, duplicated, or fabricated.

The word anomaly describes a design problem, not every failed INSERT. Rejecting a duplicate enrollment is useful integrity enforcement. Rejecting a missing required student reference may be correct for an enrollment record. The problem is using that enrollment record as the only home for course facts that have an independent lifecycle. To diagnose an insertion anomaly, ask what valid business fact needs to be represented and why the current row shape forces another fact along with it.

## Expose the mixed facts

In this simplified business rule, each course has one title and one assigned instructor. A student can enroll in many courses and a course can have many students. The following table combines course identity with participation. Its key prevents duplicate student and course pairs, but that constraint does not make the whole design suitable for storing a course catalog.

```sql
CREATE TABLE mixed_enrollment (
 student_id INT NOT NULL,
 course_id INT NOT NULL,
 course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
 instructor VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
 PRIMARY KEY (student_id,course_id)
);
INSERT INTO mixed_enrollment VALUES
 (1,10,'Databases','Meera'),
 (2,10,'Databases','Meera'),
 (1,20,'Networks','Omar');
```

The course fact Databases taught by Meera appears twice because two students enrolled. A new course 30 called Security taught by Asha cannot be represented as only a course: the table demands a student_id. Supplying NULL fails because the key is nonnullable. Supplying a fake student identifier satisfies the local shape while lying about participation. Neither workaround expresses the intended independent fact correctly.

A row with an invented student also contaminates counts, exports, notifications, and downstream joins. Application code may learn to ignore that special identifier, spreading exceptions across surfaces. A better design gives the course its own row and represents participation only when it actually exists. This resolves the cause instead of accumulating special cases around it.

## State the functional dependencies

Under the stated rule, course_id determines course_title and instructor. The pair student_id and course_id identifies an enrollment. Therefore course attributes depend on only part of the composite enrollment key. That is a partial dependency and a common reason for this insertion anomaly. Dependencies describe valid business states, not a coincidence observed in three sample rows.

If a course can have multiple instructors, the dependency to one instructor is no longer appropriate. Model teaching assignments separately or use the actual offering identity if assignments differ by term. Normalization cannot rescue an incorrectly stated business rule. First establish what a course, an offering, and an enrollment mean; then choose keys and dependencies that match those meanings.

## Separate independent entities

Create a courses relation that owns course facts, a students relation that owns student facts, and an enrollments relation that owns participation. The foreign keys require genuine parents for actual enrollments. They do not require every course to have an enrollment. This distinction lets the catalog and student participation evolve on their proper timelines.

```sql
CREATE TABLE courses (
 course_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
 instructor VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE students (
 student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 student_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
 student_id INT NOT NULL,
 course_id INT NOT NULL,
 PRIMARY KEY (student_id,course_id),
 FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(student_id),
 FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES courses(course_id)
);
INSERT INTO courses VALUES (30,'Security','Asha');
```

The final insert is now a complete, truthful fact. It creates no enrollment. A report can still reconstruct the enrollment display by joining participation to course data. Removing redundant storage does not remove the ability to present a combined report. It changes which relation authoritatively owns each fact and which relation records the relationship.

## NULL and duplicate workarounds

Allowing nullable student identifiers in a mixed table seems convenient, but it makes two different row meanings coexist: some rows are catalog entries and others are enrollments. Queries must distinguish them, and uniqueness rules become harder to express. A NULL also represents missing or inapplicable information, rather than an automatically valid independent course identity. Use a separate relation when two fact types have different keys and lifecycles.

Repeated titles are not necessarily duplicates. Different course identifiers can legitimately share a title. Conversely, repeated course identifiers with conflicting titles indicate an integrity issue under the stated dependency. Do not select an arbitrary MIN(title) to disguise that disagreement during a migration. Investigate conflicting facts and approve a resolution before populating the authoritative course relation.

A composite enrollment key still matters after decomposition. It prevents the same student and course pair appearing twice when the business allows only one enrollment per course. If retakes or term specific offerings are valid, the key must include the appropriate offering identity. Adding a surrogate row identifier alone does not enforce that business uniqueness.

## Worked lab: register a course with no students

The first task is to add Security before registration opens. The solution inserts one courses row and leaves enrollments unchanged. A query against the catalog returns course 30 even when enrollment is empty. Test that a catalog query shows all valid courses, rather than joining to participation in a way that accidentally hides empty courses.

To list courses without registrations, select from courses and use NOT EXISTS against enrollments on course_id. The expected result includes Security. This absence query does not need a fake enrollment or a NULL student row. It describes a course for which no matching participation row exists, using the schema's natural separation of facts.

```sql
SELECT c.course_id,c.course_title
FROM courses AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
 SELECT 1 FROM enrollments AS e WHERE e.course_id=c.course_id
)
ORDER BY c.course_id;
```

## Worked lab: count without losing empty courses

A second task asks for every course and its enrollment count. Start from courses, left join enrollments, and count a nonnullable enrollment component such as e.student_id. Group by the selected course columns. With courses Databases and Security and two students enrolled only in Databases, the expected counts are 2 and 0. COUNT(*) would incorrectly produce 1 for Security because the outer join creates one unmatched result row.

This lab checks whether the application can use the corrected design properly. A normalized schema still needs correct queries. An inner join can omit the very course whose independent insertion the design now supports. Test an entirely empty enrollment table, repeated titles with different identifiers, and several students on one course. Keep identity based joins rather than matching a mutable title.

## Distinguish related anomalies

The same mixed table also invites an update anomaly. If Meera changes her displayed name, every enrollment row repeating that instructor fact must change together. Updating one row leaves conflicting course descriptions. A deletion anomaly appears when the last enrollment is removed and the only stored copy of a course title disappears with it. These are different symptoms of the same misplaced ownership, and a proposed fix should check all three lifecycles.

Decomposition does not mean eliminating all repeated values everywhere. Foreign keys repeat course identifiers so relationships can be represented; that repetition is purposeful. The avoidable repetition is storing an independently determined descriptive fact in every participation row. This distinction prevents a common mistake: removing the relationship identifier in an attempt to remove redundancy, thereby making the relationship impossible to join reliably.

## Preserve existing facts during a redesign

A production correction requires an approved migration, compatibility checks, and reconciliation. Extract distinct consistent course facts, establish the target constraints, backfill participation, and compare reconstructed reports with the original data. Conflicting titles or orphan students must be surfaced rather than silently discarded. The sequence and transactional strategy depend on the real workload and cannot be inferred from this teaching fixture.

These notes demonstrate schemas and reasoned outputs without applying database changes. The immediate learning test is whether a valid course can exist without invented participation while invalid enrollments remain blocked by trusted constraints. Read [Transitive Dependency](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transitive-dependency) for another way independent facts become coupled, and [Simple Views](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/simple-views) for exposing a convenient joined interface after the facts are stored separately.
